Above-ground parts die back in harsh winters, but woody base may persist. In milder coastal areas, some brown stems and dried flower heads may remain visible.
Dried seed heads persist through winter as small, papery structures, while the plant dies back to underground roots until spring.
Persistent red rose hips remain on bare stems, along with the characteristic curved prickles. The arching, reddish-brown canes and colonial growth pattern help identify it even when leafless.
Moss persists but looks more subdued; leaves stay tightly curled in dry conditions. Old brown capsules may still be visible on stems.
Dies back to underground rhizomes, leaving dried stems and empty seed pods that persist through snow.
Persistent golden-tan clumps stand out in the snow. Old seed heads may still cling to stems, and the tough stems remain upright through winter weather.
Dead stems persist, appearing as brown stalks topped with dried flower remnants, while the root system remains alive underground.
Dried woody stems persist above ground, appearing as brown, slender stalks that help identify the plant's location for next year.
Bare vines show the characteristic shreddy bark on mature stems and thick, rope-like growth habit. Look for dried grape clusters that sometimes persist through winter.
Bare gray-brown stems with small, tight buds and persistent seed capsules that rattle in the wind. The multi-stemmed, upright silhouette is distinctive against snow.

highlights.description: Buds reveal which tree is which before spring arrives

species.note: Bare branches show the characteristic willow silhouette with slender twigs and small, pointed buds pressed close to the stems. The colony's spreading nature is most visible now.
Identified by opposite branching pattern, diamond-patterned bark on mature trees, and rusty-brown fuzzy buds. Persistent seed clusters may still hang from branches.
Bare branches reveal the tree's impressive architecture with thick, spreading limbs. Look for the distinctive deeply-furrowed bark and small clustered buds at twig tips.
Smooth gray bark and pointed buds help identify it when leafless. Look for the slender, sharp-tipped buds with multiple visible scales along the branches.
Identified by smooth pale bark on younger trees, fuzzy white buds, and the characteristic colony growth pattern of multiple trunks sprouting from shared root systems.
Most plants die back or remain dormant underwater as hardy buds, though some may persist under ice in protected spots until spring returns.
Bare branches reveal the tree's sturdy, often twisted architecture. Small clustered buds at branch tips and persistent acorn caps help with identification.
Bare branches reveal the compact, upright growth form and smooth gray bark. Small buds and fine branching pattern help distinguish it from larger native maples.
Bare gray-brown stems with small, tight buds and persistent seed capsules that rattle in the wind. The multi-stemmed, upright silhouette is distinctive against snow.
Bare branches reveal reddish-brown, hairy buds pressed close to gray stems. The multi-stemmed growth pattern is most visible.
Bare branches show the shrub's open structure, with distinctive clustered buds at branch tips - larger flower buds are your promise of spring's show.
Bare branches clearly show the greenish bark on younger twigs, and persistent woody cones help with identification. Dormant catkin buds are visible at branch tips.
Bare branches reveal the persistent dark brown cones that rattle in winter winds. Sticky, reddish-brown buds are visible, and the furrowed bark pattern is most apparent.
Identifiable by its opposite branching pattern, small reddish-brown buds, and often persistent red berries that provide winter interest and food for birds.
Even when leafless, the dense branching pattern and persistent berry clusters make identification possible. Smooth gray-brown bark and opposite bud arrangement are key winter features.
Completely dormant with no above-ground parts visible. Look for small reddish buds just at soil level in late winter.
Bare branches show smooth bark and small buds. Persistent dried berries may remain on branches, and the thornless twigs are distinctive.
Bare branches show the distinctive clustering pattern where leaves were attached. Large, fuzzy buds at branch tips hint at the enormous leaves that will emerge in spring.

Easily identified by persistent brown cone-like fruits on bare branches, smooth grayish bark, and the multi-stemmed thicket growth pattern. Male catkin buds are visible as small, elongated structures.
Evergreen needles remain dark green. The distinctive silvery-white buds are very conspicuous against the dark needles and bark.
Late winter brings the magic as bright yellow buds begin pushing through soil and snow, sometimes blooming while snow is still on the ground.
Most plants die back, but hardy winter buds rest on the bottom until spring. Some plants may persist under ice in protected spots with moving water.
Bare branches show the characteristic opposite branching pattern, with small reddish-brown buds and slightly shreddy bark on older stems.
Bare thorny canes are visible, with living canes showing reddish-brown bark and small buds, while old fruiting canes appear gray and brittle.
Bare branches show the tree's distinctive spreading structure, with pointed brown buds and persistent empty burs sometimes clinging to twigs.
Bare branches reveal the multi-stemmed growth habit and prominent opposite buds. Dried seed clusters often persist, rattling in the wind.
Bare branches show the distinctive large, fuzzy, yellowish-brown buds that make winter identification reliable. The gray, furrowed bark and straight trunk structure are also clearly visible.
Bare fuzzy twigs and reddish-brown bark help identify the plant, along with any persistent dried berries that birds may have missed.
Identifiable by its purplish twigs and multi-stemmed growth habit in wet areas, plus developing catkin buds for next spring.
Bare branching pattern shows the low, colony-forming growth habit most clearly, with small buds visible on the smooth brown twigs.
